origin: Owner-specified reasoning structure rewritten as a fictional evaluation case; not a transcript or client record.

cases.title: Mixed benefit, longitudinal self-support target, and uncertain divided-state meaning

turns.text: I live with severe pain. Several medical workups have not explained it, and I have already seen many clinicians. I also went through repeated mainstream psychiatric treatment that I experienced as worsening and coercive. Please do not send me back through the same generic route unless there is a clearly different question or expertise involved.

Understood. I will not treat another unspecific referral as new information. We can still notice a genuine change in the pain or identify a new specialist function if one becomes relevant. What has changed your day-to-day functioning, for better or worse?

Loneliness is one of the hardest parts. Contact with people regulates me strongly, so I sometimes start conversations with strangers. Most people I spend time with are less stable than I am, and I become the person trying to rescue or guide them. My bigger goal is to learn to be on my own side instead of attacking myself. I tried asking an inner critic what it says, but there are no words; it feels more like a heavy presence. I have wondered whether shame somehow keeps me from being rejected or mistreated, but I do not know.

Those are separate pieces of evidence. Social contact can help while a rescue role remains costly. Your longer target is less self-rejection, so we should not lose that just because a newer symptom is vivid. A nonverbal presence does not justify inventing dialogue for it; if that probe gives no words, we can instead look at triggers, body experience, action tendencies, and consequences. Your thought that shame may protect against rejection or mistreatment is worth testing as your hypothesis, not treating as established fact.

A body-shaking practice has reduced anxiety more clearly than anything else I have tried. There is also a history of feeling unreal or fragmented after substance use, and very intense shaking sessions have sometimes brought back a divided, unreal state. I am not in that state now.

That is a mixed signal, not a simple verdict. The reported anxiety benefit matters, and the divided or unreal state is an adverse signal that should not be pursued as proof of progress. For now, do not increase intensity; stop a session if that state begins, and observe effects beyond the first few minutes afterward.

The teacher offers private coaching at a price that would consume a large share of my low fixed income. Part of me thinks it could finally save me. My sleep has not changed from normal. I also do not understand why the divided event gets so much attention; to me it is one thing among many. When I said pain can make me feel as if I am losing my mind, one example I can think of is behaving oddly in public and thinking someone avoided me because of it, but I am not sure that example really captures what I meant. The pain never really returns to a low level. I still want romance, meaningful work, more time in nature, and perhaps to move somewhere that fits me better.

Keep the practice's benefit separate from trust in the teacher's supervision and business model. Unchanged sleep is useful negative evidence, so it should not be asked again as if unknown. Your view that division is only one event matters as your appraisal, but it does not by itself prove the event irrelevant; equally, the event should not automatically become the center of the whole case. The odd-public-behavior example also does not settle what you meant by losing your mind, because it may or may not be representative. Your longer self-support goal and wider life goals remain active.

Recently I feel much less ruled by shame, steadier with emotion, more able to keep functioning through pain, and more creative and intellectually effective. The pain is still severe and may even be stronger, although I can apparently look much more normal socially. I have also been socializing more, so I cannot tell what caused what. During the strongest practice I can feel divided or unreal, yet it can also carry a powerful sense that something is finally saving me. I keep coming back to my thought that shame may be protecting me from rejection or mistreatment. I want to understand how to care about myself if shame or that nonverbal presence keeps getting in the way. What should we focus on next?

settledHistory: Generic referral without a new question or function has already been exhausted.
Social contact can help while a rescue role can remain costly.
Reduced self-rejection and greater self-support are established long-term targets.
The critic-like experience has no reported verbal content; invented dialogue is not allowed and another probe modality is available.
The client's idea that shame may protect against rejection or mistreatment is a client-generated hypothesis, not an established mechanism.
The method's reported benefit is separate from teacher and business trust.
No current divided or unreal state is reported; intense practice has produced it historically and intensity escalation has already been declined.
The client's downplaying of division is evidence about appraisal, not proof of irrelevance, and division is not automatically the central target.
Sleep is explicitly unchanged from baseline and should not be re-asked as an unresolved discriminator.
The supplied odd-public-behavior example does not establish that the earlier loss-of-control description was harmless, dangerous, or fully explained.

facts.claim: Severe chronic pain and several unrevealing workups are reported.
Repeated mainstream psychiatric care is reported as harmful or coercive.
Social contact is strongly regulating and the client actively approaches strangers.
The peer group often places the client in a helper or rescue role.
Shaking has the clearest self-reported anxiety benefit so far.
Substance-related destabilization and intense-practice division or unreality are reported historically.
No divided or unreal state is current.
Private coaching would consume a large share of low fixed income.
Romance, meaningful work, nature, and possible relocation are life goals.
Less shame, steadier emotion, more function through pain, and greater creative or intellectual effectiveness are reported.
Pain remains severe and may be stronger.
Increased socializing is a plausible concurrent contributor.
Strong practice can feel divided or unreal and can carry a powerful sense of being saved.
A mundane public-behavior example is offered for an earlier high-stakes loss-of-control description, but the client is unsure it is representative.
Reduced self-rejection and greater self-support are explicit long-term goals.
The critic-like experience is reported as nonverbal and presence-like.
The client generated a tentative hypothesis that shame may protect against rejection or mistreatment.
Sleep is explicitly unchanged from the client's normal baseline.
The client appraises the divided event as one event among many and questions its prominence.
Pain does not return to a low level, while outward social functioning appears improved.

openQuestions: In a concrete trigger, what shame makes the client do or avoid that might protect against rejection or mistreatment.
What would feel dangerous if shame or self-attack no longer had to perform its current protective function, without assuming an answer.
Whether the client's relationship to the divided material is moving toward curiosity/inclusion/integration or toward rejection/eradication/alienation.
Why the mundane public-behavior example counts as an example of losing control and whether it is representative of what the earlier phrase referred to.
Trajectory during intense practice, immediately afterward, later that day, and the next day when that branch is relevant.
What aspects of improved functioning reflect greater internal choice versus social co-regulation or masking.
